Ūrdhvaretas & Brahmacharya: The Yogic View of Sexual Energy and Willpower

A compassionate look at Brahmacharya and ūrdhvaretas — the yogic view of sexual energy — and how these ideas can gently support urge control.

Key Takeaways

  • •Brahmacharya is one of the yamas in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras — "conduct that leads toward the divine" — traditionally read as sexual restraint, though many modern teachers understand it more broadly as mindful, non-exploitative use of vital energy.
  • •Ūrdhvaretas describes a yogic idea of redirecting sexual and vital energy upward through the subtle body, rather than only dissipating it — a concept closely linked to Kundalini practice.
  • •Some people find these traditional frameworks genuinely supportive for urge control, including with compulsive pornography use, but they work best as one supportive lens among several, not a stand-alone cure.
  • •This is a spiritual and self-development perspective, not medical or psychological treatment — if urges feel unmanageable or distressing, working with a licensed therapist alongside any spiritual practice is a wise, ordinary step, not a failure.

If you've ever felt caught between wanting more discipline over a restless urge and not wanting to feel ashamed about it, you're in familiar territory for yogic philosophy. Long before modern conversations about screen time and compulsive habits, yogis were asking a related question: what do we do with the sheer force of sexual and vital energy that moves through a human body? Two old ideas — Brahmacharya and ūrdhvaretas — offer one thoughtful answer. Neither was designed to shame anyone. Both were designed to help a person work *with* their own energy rather than feel helplessly at its mercy.

This article is written with care, because the subject touches something private and often painful for many people. Nothing here is meant to moralize, frighten, or suggest that sexuality itself is a problem to be solved. The aim is simply to explain what these traditions actually say, and to offer a gentle, honest way they might support someone who wants steadier ground with an urge — whatever that urge is directed toward.

What Brahmacharya Actually Means

Brahmacharya is the fourth of the five yamas — the ethical restraints Patanjali lists at the very start of the Yoga Sutras, alongside non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-attachment. The word itself breaks down as *Brahman* (the divine, the absolute) and *charya* (conduct, or a way of moving through life) — literally, "conduct that leads toward the divine." For centuries this was interpreted quite strictly, especially for monks and dedicated renunciates, as complete sexual restraint or celibacy, understood as a way of conserving energy for spiritual practice.

Many contemporary teachers, myself included, read Brahmacharya more broadly for a modern householder's life. Rather than a blanket rule against sexuality, it's understood as mindful, non-exploitative use of vital energy — sexual energy included, but also the energy we spend on ambition, speech, attention, and desire generally. Seen this way, Brahmacharya isn't asking "do you abstain?" so much as "are you spending this energy consciously, or is it spending you?" That reframe matters a great deal for anyone who has felt trapped by a habit they didn't consciously choose.

What Ūrdhvaretas Means

Ūrdhvaretas (from *ūrdhva*, "upward," and *retas*, "seed" or vital fluid) is a more specific and more mystical idea within the same broad territory. Classical yogic and tantric texts describe it as a state in which sexual and vital energy is deliberately redirected — "raised" — upward through the subtle body, rather than only released or dissipated outward. It draws on the same subtle-body map used in Kundalini practice: a central channel (sushumna) running along the spine, through which awakened energy is said to rise toward higher centers of awareness.

It's worth being honest that ūrdhvaretas is described in the texts as an advanced, rare accomplishment — not a quick technique or a switch you flip. For most practitioners today, it's less useful as a literal goal and more useful as a felt image: energy that might otherwise scatter into a compulsive loop can instead be met, breathed with, and redirected into steadiness, creativity, or focus. You don't need to achieve some final mystical state for that reframe to be genuinely helpful in an ordinary week.

Why People Turn to This for Urge Control

It makes sense that someone wrestling with compulsive pornography use or a sexual habit that feels out of their own control might be drawn to these ideas. Where a purely willpower-based approach can feel like white-knuckling against an enemy inside yourself, the yogic framing offers something gentler: the urge isn't a flaw to be crushed, it's energy — real, morally neutral, and redirectable. That shift in language alone helps many people move from self-punishment toward self-partnership, which tends to be a far more sustainable place to work from.

One supportive lens among several — not a replacement for professional help

It's important to be direct about this: Brahmacharya and ūrdhvaretas are a spiritual and self-development framework, not medical or psychological treatment. They can sit comfortably alongside therapy, addiction counseling, or medical care — they are not a substitute for it. If compulsive sexual behavior or pornography use is causing real distress, conflict, or feels genuinely unmanageable, please consider also speaking with a licensed therapist or counselor who specializes in this area. Reaching out for that kind of support is a sign of self-respect, not a sign that the spiritual path has failed you — the two work well together.

What a Modern, Non-Shaming Practice Can Look Like

None of this requires monastic renunciation. A modern practice inspired by these ideas tends to have a few simple, humane components, built around awareness first, willpower second.

  • Mindful awareness of triggers. Before an urge can be redirected, it has to be noticed. Simply naming "this is the restless feeling, this is the trigger" — without judgment — creates a small gap where a different choice becomes possible.
  • Breathwork to redirect restless energy. Slow, steady breathing (the same nervous-system tools used in pranayama) is one of the most immediate ways to meet a surge of restless energy in the body rather than act on it automatically. Even ninety seconds of unhurried breath can be enough to let an urge crest and pass.
  • A visualization of energy moving upward. Picturing energy rising gently along the spine — the felt image behind ūrdhvaretas — gives the mind somewhere constructive to place attention, instead of leaving it with nowhere to go but the old habit.
  • A support structure, like a streak or accountability practice. Tracking progress — a streak, a journal, a check-in with a friend or teacher — turns an invisible internal struggle into something visible and shared, which most people find far easier to stay motivated with.
  • Patience with setbacks. A slip is information, not proof of failure. The traditions this practice draws from were built for a whole lifetime of steady effort, not a single unbroken streak — treating a setback as data to learn from, rather than evidence you're beyond help, is itself part of the practice.

A Framework, Not a Verdict

Brahmacharya and ūrdhvaretas were never meant to hand anyone a verdict about their worth. They were meant to hand people a relationship with their own energy — one built on awareness, patience, and redirection rather than suppression or shame. If you're working with an urge that feels bigger than you right now, that relationship is worth building slowly, with whatever mix of breath, practice, community, and professional support actually helps. There is no failing version of trying.

Energy is never destroyed, only redirected. The work is not to fight the current, but to learn where it can flow.

— Traditional yogic teaching
